Messages.Author: Dave Andrews
Messages.Body:
I have a question about card wording. Once, a while back, I was playing with
some friends and I called for a Rumors of Gehenna vote. I named myself as the
person who would get to play 2 masters if the vote passed, and my friends
complained. They said I had to name at least 2 players to get the benefit,
because the card said "Name a set of Methuselahs..." Now, as a math minor, I
know a set can consist of any number of things, including only 1 thing or even
0 things, but they argued that it meant more than 1. Later that night we
could WotC customer service for their opinion, and the rep on the phone said,
"Well, set would usually refer to more than 1, so it has to be more than 1."
I thought this was pretty silly, because what something >usually< means
doesn't really matter; in a CCG you're probably gonna be pushing a card's
wording to extremes. But we've played it that way without problem. Now I'm
unhappy, though, 'cause i just opened my first booster of V:TES and I see the
new Sabbat Threat says "Choose a set..." Does this mean I can't call ST to
give a threat counter to just 1 person?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Dave Andrews
S2...@nmu.edu

Yes. I understand the fact that math may tell us that a set can mean any number,
however, the common interpretation for the great mass of the population is that
number means 2. As in a pair... a set. It has been interpreted as meaning 2 or
more in this case. This also serves as a safety valve for game balance since you
can't just shalack whoever you want without carefully considering your move,
unlike Magic which involves no thought what so ever. Besides, by requiring 2 or
more you just might have to do some political negotiating to get your vote passed
if there are other votes on the table... which adds more intrigue to the game,
non?

No. A set (in Jyhad and anywhere else) is zero, one, or more things.

You may name zero Methuselahs with either Rumors or Sabbat Threat (this
will result in a NULL vote - a vote that does nothing but pass or fail).

You may name exactly one Methuselah, and the expected result will be true -
SVM means that the named Methuselah has (two Master/another Threat counter).

Or you may name two or more Methuselahs with the unarguable result.

Generally (in the real world) a set of zero or one isn't interesting to
call a set - too many words. A set of zero is nothing, and usaully refered
to as such. A set of one thing is simply referred to as that one thing.

That brevity is the norm should not be taken as an indication that the
verbose is untrue.

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Grrr.... As a math _major_, this gets me upset. What "people usually
think something is becuase they don't know better" and what "something
actually is" are two different things. I would _really_ like to see an
official ruling using the (mathematical) definition of set, i.e. a
collection of distinct (different) objects. Thus, the same Methuselah
could not be included twice in the same set, and you could, of course,
choose 0 or 1 Methuselah for your set.

Tom?

Messages.Author: Steven Bauer
Messages.Body:
I have always played with the house rule that you can't play cards just
to burn them. They must have some effect.

No, allowing sets of zero does not unbalance the game, but it does not
add anything to the game either(IMO). It would have been very nice if
wizards of the cost defined set in the rules but there are a lot of things
left unsaid in the rules.

I also don't play with the rule on extra-strike cards that lets you use as many
as you wanted, with only the first having any effect.

I also don't play with the rule that you can use wake's to untap with out an
intention to block or use intercept.

--Steve
